Operator:
Good morning, and welcome to the AeroTech Industries Third Quarter 2024 Earnings Conference Call. All participants will be in listen-only mode. After today's presentation, there will be an opportunity to ask questions. As a reminder, instructions for queuing up will be given at that time. Please note this event is being recorded.

I would now like to turn the conference over to Sarah Thompson, VP of Investor Relations. Please go ahead.

Sarah Thompson:
Thank you, Operator, and good morning, everyone. Welcome to AeroTech Industries' Third Quarter 2024 Earnings Conference Call. Joining me today are Michael Reynolds, Chief Executive Officer; John Ramirez, Chief Financial Officer; Lisa Chen, Chief Operating Officer; Dr. Elena Vasquez, Chief Technology Officer; and Robert Kline, Chief Strategy Officer.

Before we begin, I'd like to remind you that this call contains forward-looking statements. Please refer to our SEC filings for a complete discussion of risks and uncertainties.

Michael Reynolds:
Thank you, Sarah, and good morning. AeroTech Industries delivered a solid performance in the third quarter, demonstrating the resilience of our business model and the strength of our diversified portfolio across commercial aviation, defense and space, and services. Our priorities remain focused on executing our strategy, driving operational excellence, and delivering value to our shareholders. Today, I'll cover several key areas shaping our outlook.

Let me start with the key assumptions underlying our guidance. We're reaffirming our full-year 2024 guidance, with revenue expected between $28.5 billion and $29.5 billion, reflecting 9% to 12% organic growth year-over-year. Adjusted earnings per share are targeted at $12.80 to $13.40, while segment operating margins expand by 50 to 100 basis points to 12.5% to 13.0%. Free cash flow is projected at $3.2 billion to $3.6 billion, including $1.1 billion in pension contributions. These figures are built on a solid foundation from our $125 billion backlog, which provides about 4.2 years of revenue visibility at the midpoint, supported by a book-to-bill ratio of 1.1x.

In our Defense and Space segment, which makes up 45% of our FY2024 revenue mix, we anticipate 10% to 13% growth. This hinges on steady U.S. Department of Defense top-line funding increases of 4% to 5% under the FY2025 National Defense Authorization Act, now at $895 billion. We're counting on seamless execution of fixed-price contracts for the F-35 Lightning II Joint Strike Fighter, assuming deliveries of 180 to 200 aircraft from Lots 17 through 19 in low-rate initial production, covering our aerostructures and mission systems shares. Production rates at Lockheed Martin sites are expected to rise 2% to 3%, backed by our titanium forgings ramp-up from the Oklahoma City facility, now achieving 95% on-time delivery as a Tier 1 supplier.

Geopolitical tensions in the Indo-Pacific, such as China's J-20 expansions and Taiwan Strait operations, should sustain Foreign Military Sales under the U.S. State Department's $90 billion industry-wide backlog. This benefits our hypersonic efforts, including the AGM-183A Air-Launched Rapid Response Weapon Phase 3 boosters, where we project 15% revenue growth from additive-manufactured components that cut part count by 40% using laser powder bed fusion, delivering 20% cost reductions on prototypes. For Space, we're taking a cautious view on NASA Artemis delays shifting SLS Block 1B core stage deliveries to Q4 2025, balanced by $2.5 billion in commercial launches with SpaceX Falcon Heavy and ULA Vulcan Centaur. Our uncrewed systems, like MQ-9 Reaper sustainment and loyal wingman drones similar to the XQ-58 Valkyrie, incorporate a 12% NATO spending increase in Europe, with 25% of FY2025 bookings linked to AUKUS Pillar II technology transfers for autonomous undersea vehicles. Potential continuing resolutions delaying DoD funds by 30 to 60 days have been tested, impacting segment EPS by just 1%. Margins here are set at 11.5% to 12.0%, with 150 basis points from favorable learning curves on F-35 fuselages offset by 50 basis points of 4.5% labor inflation.

Shifting to Commercial Aviation, 35% of our revenue mix and our primary growth driver, OEM revenue is guided to $9.8 billion to $10.2 billion, up 15% year-over-year, based on narrowbody production increases amid strong air traffic recovery. Global revenue passenger kilometers are forecasted to rise 7% to 8% according to IATA, with load factors at 83% to 85%. Boeing's 737 MAX line rate should reach 42 per month by year-end from 31 currently, and Airbus A320neo family at 50 per month, pushing our wingbox and nacelle deliveries to 280 to 310 units—a 20% sequential increase from Q3. Widebody rates are steadier: Boeing 787-10 at 5 per month and A350 at 6, factoring in 10% supply chain improvements on geared turbofan engine modules from RTX's Pratt & Whitney after their Q3 fixes hit 85% on-time delivery. We've modeled a 15% shortfall in LEAP-1B engines from CFM International, countered by digital twin predictive spares that have shortened MRO lead times 25%. Sustainability plays a role, with 20% of composites qualifying for sustainable aviation fuel blends under ICAO CORSIA Phase 2, generating $150 million in renewable energy certificate credits for FY2025. North America accounts for 55% of OEM bookings from Delta and United upgrades; Asia-Pacific 30%, aided by IndiGo's 500-plus A320neo orders and China's COMAC C919 ramp, discounted 10% for certification hurdles. Margins target 10.0% to 10.5%, with 200 basis points from volume leverage offset by 3% titanium inflation—VSMPO-AVISMA at $35 per kilogram—and 4% skilled labor rises at Everett and Charleston.

Services and Aftermarket, 20% of the mix and our highest margins at 18% to 19%, should grow 8% to 10% to $5.8 billion, driven by aging fleets and 11.5 hours per day utilization per Cirium. MRO shop visits for CFM56 and LEAP narrowbodies rise to 22% from 20% due to deferred post-COVID work. TrueChoice PowerBy-the-Hour deals with Lufthansa Technik and ST Engineering achieve 90% utilization across 15 global centers. AI and machine learning in our Engine Health Management platform cut unplanned removals 15%, adding $300 million in annuity revenue. MENA grows 25% from Etihad and Qatar widebody C-checks; Europe 12% from Ryanair V2500 overhauls.

Cross-cutting factors include supply chain normalization by mid-2025 at 92% supplier on-time delivery versus 82% in Q2, via a $500 million Supplier Recovery Fund and dual-sourcing avionics ASICs. FX assumes USD at 1.08 to EUR and 145 to JPY, with 100 basis points stronger dollar trimming revenue $200 million, 70% hedged. Inflation at CPI 2.5% to 3.0%, materials 4%, labor 4.2%, offset by 3% productivity from Factory 4.0. CapEx at $1.4 billion for hypersonic test beds and A350 composites automation. Tax at 22%; net interest $450 million post-refinancing. This embeds our Fortress Balance Sheet at 1.8x net debt to EBITDA, enabling tuck-in M&A like a $1.2 billion hypersonics fab in Q1 2025. No major black swans assumed, but war-gamed for $0.50 EPS hit from a 737 MAX halt. With 75% of FY2024 revenue contracted, we're set in a resilient A&D market with defense tailwinds, commercial backlog conversion, and services stability.

Next, the geopolitical factors affecting defense spending. This macro tailwind is pivotal for us at AeroTech Industries, leaders in next-generation fighters, missile defense, and unmanned systems. SIPRI data shows global defense spending hit $2.44 trillion in 2023, up 6.8% real terms—the biggest jump since the Cold War—with 5-7% growth projected for 2024 as budgets shift to peer competition. Our Defense segment grew 14% quarter-over-quarter to $2.8 billion in Q3, with $48 billion funded backlog up 22% year-over-year.

In Europe, Russia-Ukraine has spurred NATO's 2% GDP push—23 of 32 members compliant. Germany's €100 billion Zeitenwende fund directed €8.6 billion to procurement, including 35 more F-35A from partners like us supplying AN/APG-85 AESA radars. Poland's $10 billion army expansion to 300,000 troops includes 1,000 K2 tanks and HIMARS, lifting artillery 40%. Our European revenues rose 28% year-over-year; AGM-179 JAGM PGMs surged 150% from Ukraine stockpile depletions. We've doubled PGM lines in Camden, Arkansas, to 12,000 units yearly.

Indo-Pacific sees China-Taiwan as the main threat, with Beijing's $292 billion budget up 7.2% and DF-17 hypersonics prompting $9.1 billion Pacific Deterrence Initiative, up 11% for JADC2. Our NGAD-derived CCA drones won a $2.4 billion IDIQ for 150 units, ramping low-rate production Q4. AUKUS's $368 billion over 30 years brought $1.2 billion for Tomahawk Block V. Japan's 2% GDP by 2027 includes 147 F-35s, our avionics 15% of value; this drives 35% ISR backlog growth, AI autonomy cutting sortie costs 25% in sims.

Middle East: Israel-Hamas and Iran proxies boost Iron Dome/Arrow. Israel's $24 billion budget up 25% has $3.5 billion U.S. aid for interceptors; our SkyHunter radar for Tamir hit 95% intercepts. Saudi Vision 2030's $75 billion over five years favors Patriot PAC-3 MSE, up 40% sales; GCC up 12% via FMS.

U.S. FY2025 NDAA at $895 billion—2% over inflation—plus $110 billion supplements for Ukraine/Israel/Taiwan fund B-21 Raider at 2-3/year, F-35 TR-3, Replicator's 1,000 drones. Our DoD primes are 65%, F-35 $1.1 billion annualized.

Trends: munitions replenishment—Ukraine ate 2 million 155mm shells; we're at 100,000/month via Oklahoma. Tech race—$1.2 billion IRAD for HAWC boosters eyes $15 billion FY25. Allied interoperability—GCAP/GCAS favor our C4ISR. Risks like 20% rare earth inflation mitigated by dual-sourcing, $500 million hedges. Targeting 12-15% organic growth to 2026, ROIC to 18%.

Moving to our book-to-bill ratio, overall and by segment—a vital indicator in our backlog-driven industry with programs like F-35 sustainment and hypersonics. Q3 overall was 1.18x, ninth straight quarter over 1.0x, up from 1.12x prior year: $4.2 billion new orders versus $3.55 billion revenue, backlog to record $78.5 billion, up 12%. Core ex one-time spares: 1.14x.

Commercial Aerospace (32% revenue): 1.06x, up from 0.98x, $1.1 billion bookings including LEAP aftermarket for 737 MAX/A320neo from Delta/Emirates. Slots 85% committed to 2027; 777X delays shift to 787 sustainment. North America 1.10x, APAC 0.95x offset by COMAC/SAF JVs.

Defense Systems (45%): 1.28x, flat sequential, up from 1.22x YoY; $2.0 billion bookings led by $850 million F-35 AN/APG-81 upgrades with Lockheed, PAC-3 MSE. FY25 DoD $850 billion, 6% missile defense; Europe 1.35x from NATO €100 billion Ukraine aid. $250 million digital twins for directed energy/IFPC Phase 2.

Space & Missiles (18%): 1.32x from 1.25x; $950 million bookings vs. $720 million, $600 million NASA Orion propulsion, $400 million DARPA HAWC hypersonics. Backlog $15.2 billion, 70% funded; U.S. 1.40x, international 1.15x. Proliferated LEO with SpaceX Starshield.

Aftermarket & Services (5%, 22% EBITDA): 0.92x from 0.97x; $150 million including KC-46 PBL. Funded backlog $8.1 billion.

Backlog 3.5x annual revenue, pricing +150bps margins. $500 million reshoring for 95% OTD; Q4 1.15-1.20x via GE JV, F-35 Block 4. Positions us in $900 billion A&D at 5% CAGR to 2030.

Now, performance of our priority defense programs, driving 75% Defense revenue at $3.2 billion Q3, up 18% YoY/5% QoQ, $52 billion funded backlog. Pillars: NGAD, hypersonics, IAMD, uncrewed. FY24 DoD $849 billion aids PDI/Ukraine.

NGAD/fifth-gen: $4.2 billion LRIP for digital twins/CCAs, YTD $7.8 billion. 28 F-35 Block 4 deliveries, $1.1 billion revenue, margins 13.2% (+220bps) on composites/AESA. AI mission planning TRL 8, OT&E at Edwards. NATO/UK/Italy $1.5 billion sustainment; Japan 42 F-35A/year. Dual-source titanium cuts leads 35% for FRP FY25.

Hypersonics: $4.7 billion DoD; Black Widow scramjet Mayhem ground tests Mach 7+ at White Sands. $850 million Q2 (+45% YoY), $2.9 billion Army LRHW IDIQ. Backlog $12.4 billion, 1.7x book-to-bill. Additive TPS -28% costs, 50/year by 2026. AUKUS/Boeing/BAE; ME counter-hypersonics. Margins 14.8%, fixed-price CPI.

IAMD: $950 million (+22% YoY), PAC-3 MSE/NGI GMD. 320 MSEs for Ukraine $1.2 billion; Poland/Romania $800 million fire control. Aegis GaN radars 98% kills Pacific Fury. Backlog $15.2 billion, $3.1 billion NGI Lot 1. Margins 12.5%, LEAN -18% labor. Saudi $3.5 billion THAAD-like; NATO Eastern Flank 15% CAGR. $250 million microelectronics fab/CHIPS.

Uncrewed/C4ISR: MQ-Next/loyal wingman $450 million (+30%), $1.8 billion Navy CCA, backlog $8.9 billion. 50+ swarm demos TRL 9. JADC2/Palantir $300 million, margins 11.9% (+150bps).

98% cost/97% schedule per DCMA; $1.2 billion digital engineering -40% iterations. Ukraine doubles munitions; China/Taiwan $9.9 billion PDI. Q3 Defense $3.4-3.6 billion, FY 16-18% growth, 12.5-13.0% margins; backlog $65 billion YE.

On revenue and earnings guidance by segment for Q4 2024 and FY2025. FY2024 revenue $28.5-29.0 billion (+8% midpoint), op profit $4.8-5.0 billion (17.0% margins +50bps), $125 billion backlog. Q4 revenue $7.4-7.6 billion, op profit $1.25-1.30 billion.

Aeronautics (42%): Q3 28 F-47 NGAD analogs/12 GAD-900. Q4 $3.1-3.2 billion (+12% QoQ) F-47 LRIP Lot 5/C-130J. FY25 $12.0-12.5 billion (+10%), 11.5-12.0% margins (+ from 10.8%) digital thread -18% F-47 time Fort Worth. RPKs 105% 2019; Boeing delays. $450 million SAF GAD-900. U.S. $849 billion FY25; Tempest GCAP watch.

Missiles & Defense (28%): Q3 $2.3 billion JASSM-ER/Patriot Ukraine. Q4 $2.2-2.3 billion (+15% YoY), op $650-680 million (29%). FY25 $8.0-8.3 billion (+14%), 28.5%. Backlog $42 billion, LRHW $1.2 billion. Inventories -20-30% Ukraine/CSIS. APAC $900 million AUKUS/Japan; ME $500 million Israel/Saudi. $300 million R&D GaN lasers 300kW mid-2025 vs. Northrop.

Space (15%): Q3 SDA Tranche 2. Q4 $1.1-1.15 billion (+9%), op $220-240 million (20.5%). FY25 $4.2-4.5 billion (+18%), 20.0-20.5%. $18 billion backlog NASA CLPS/Golden Dome. SpaceX Starship; GADLaunch 15% $7 billion small-launch. NSSL $2.5 billion; $200 million robotics/Maxar $1 billion sustainment 2030.

Services (15%): Q3 $1.1 billion F-35/KC-46. Q4 $1.0-1.05 billion, op $280-300 million (28%). FY25 $4.5-4.7 billion (+12%), 27.5%. $15 billion backlog PBH F-16. MRO +7% Oliver Wyman; AI PHM +12% uptime. NATO $600 million UK/Poland Typhoon.

Disciplined amid titanium/avionics; FCF $3.5 billion 2024, $1.2 billion repurchases, 10% dividend hike.

Finally, the defense budget outlook and its impact. U.S. FY2025 DoD $849.8 billion (+4.1%), procurement +5.2% $167.5 billion, RDT&E +10.1% $145 billion for JADC2/hypersonics/CCA. NATO $1.47 trillion 2024 (+9%); Europe Ukraine aid; Japan $59 billion (+7.5%) hypersonics; AUKUS subs/strike. U.S. 65% revenue, international FMS/DCS 25% (up from 20%); ME +15% bookings; LRASM $2.4 billion Indo-Pacific.

$128 billion backlog ($72 billion funded), 4x TTM revenue; 85% FY2025 booked. Defense 68% Q2, FY25 16-18% growth > sector 8-10%. Fighter/NGAD $1.2 billion digital, $2.3 billion RDT&E; F-35 Lot 16 156 aircraft $850 million 12-14% margins. Hypersonics +28% $4.7 billion, ARRW TRL-6 $10 billion HACM; $3.1 billion bookings. CCA $3.3 billion MQ-20; Space Force $30 billion ESS +20%.

70% fixed-price new awards, EBIT 13.2% Q2 (+150bps). $500 million titanium offtakes. FY25 defense $28-30 billion, +$1.20-1.40 EPS. $50 billion 5-year pipeline.

We are particularly excited about the recent advancements in our hypersonic missile systems program and its potential to revolutionize rapid response capabilities for our future growth. We are seeing strong demand for our defense systems, and our commercial aerospace business is recovering steadily.

John Ramirez:
Thank you, Michael. Now, let's turn to the financials. In Q3, we reported revenue of $7.2 billion, representing a 12% increase year-over-year. Our earnings per share were $3.25. We continue to maintain a strong balance sheet with $4.5 billion in cash and equivalents. Our guidance for the full year remains unchanged. We are actively managing our costs and investing in key growth initiatives. We are also focused on returning capital to shareholders through dividends and share repurchases.

Our specific financial highlights include:
* Gross Margin: 22.5%
* Operating Income: $1.6 billion
* Free Cash Flow: $850 million

Lisa Chen:
Thank you, John. Operationally, we have seen significant improvements in our supply chain management, allowing us to increase production rates on key programs like F-35 aerostructures and hypersonic components. We are also investing in automation and digital technologies to improve efficiency and reduce costs. Specifically, our Factory 4.0 initiatives have boosted productivity by 3% across sites, with dual-sourcing titanium and avionics achieving 92% on-time delivery, and reshoring rare earths via a $500 million fund mitigating Ukraine-related disruptions.

Dr. Elena Vasquez:
Thank you, Lisa. On the technology front, we're making significant strides in our next-generation propulsion systems, including scramjet engines for hypersonics and GaN radars for IAMD. We anticipate these advancements will give us a competitive edge in the years to come. More specifically, AI/ML for predictive health management has reduced unplanned removals 15%, digital twins cut design iterations 40%, and additive manufacturing slashes hypersonic TPS costs 28%, positioning us for NGAD CCAs and JADC2 integrations at TRL 8-9.

Operator:
Thank you. We will now begin the question and answer session. Our first question comes from Josh Hunter with Goldman Sachs. Please go ahead.

Josh Hunter:
Good morning. Can you provide more color on the book-to-bill trends by segment and how they inform backlog conversion?

Michael Reynolds:
Certainly, Josh. As Michael outlined, our 1.18x overall reflects robust demand, with Defense at 1.28x from F-35 and PAC-3 wins, and Space 1.32x on Artemis and hypersonics. This grows backlog to $78.5 billion, converting steadily at 25-30% annually, supporting multi-year visibility.

Operator:
Our next question comes from Emily Carter with Morgan Stanley. Please go ahead.

Emily Carter:
Hi, I'm curious about geopolitical risks and their potential impact on your defense outlook?

John Ramirez:
Emily, the structural shifts—Europe's NATO surge, Indo-Pacific PDI, Middle East IAMD—drive 12-15% growth, with $48 billion funded backlog insulating us. We've hedged supply inflation and stress-tested CRs; no material FY24 hit expected.

Operator:
Our next question comes from David Lee with Barclays. Please go ahead.

David Lee:
Regarding the key assumptions in your guidance, particularly supply chain and commercial ramps?

Dr. Elena Vasquez:
David, our assumptions bake in 92% supplier OTD by mid-2025, Boeing/Airbus rates to 42/50 monthly, and digital twins mitigating LEAP shortfalls. Defense execution on F-35 lots and hypersonics remains flawless at 95-98% on schedule.

Michael Reynolds:
Thank you for your questions. In closing, I'm confident in our ability to navigate the current environment and deliver long-term value to our shareholders. We remain focused on our strategic priorities, operational excellence, and innovation.

Sarah Thompson:
Thank you for joining us today. This concludes our earnings call.

Operator:
This concludes today's conference call. Thank you for participating. You may now disconnect.
